So with lettuce being a cool crop, it's always good to keep them from getting too much sun. Idk if yours get full sun or not; I'm thinking not because of your area. So it's likely not dry wilt because it's thirsty or because of excessive heat. When my lettuce leaves wilted, it was always one of two things. Either too much sun or too much water. If it was too hot, I had to use a shade cloth, otherwise the leaves would be dry and crispy. If it was being overwatered, the leaves tend to look like yours and I would just peel off the damaged outer leaves and do less deep watering to prevent disease. Another way to see if it's getting too much water is to check if the leaves have any browning or gray patches or you see decaying root. It could be there's not enough drainage from watering due to the soil. That can cause root rot which usually looks like mushy black or brown mushy roots underneath. You could just snip off the withered part and only water once a day early morning, but water every day since they require frequent watering vs deep watering which leads to root rot or diseases like leaf drop. That can cause the plant to not be able to absorb the water. 🤷‍♀️ Or I could just be blowing air and it's none of the above and your lettuce is fine! 😄 Hard to say, but I would just cut of that outer leaf, check that the water is being absorbed into the soil after watering and see how it goes. 🙂 The soil is a good indication of how much to water. Hope that helps!

This Garlic Soy Sauce Pasta is an easy & quick Chinese soy sauce pasta recipe made with green onions, garlic, bean sprouts, and onion. This soy sauce pasta dish is inspired by the cantonese supreme soy sauce noodles, which are pan-fried and served at dim sum restaurants.  

The key ingredients are linguine, light and dark soy sauce, green onions, garlic, bean sprouts, and onion. If you don’t have dark soy sauce, just use 3/4 light soy and 1/4 sugar.  

I often use spaghetti or linguine instead of Chinese noodles because it’s a bit cheaper.  

Ingredients:  
SERVES 2  
\* 5 oz linguini pasta (140g)  
\* ½ tbsp soy sauce  
\* 1 tbsp dark soy sauce  
\* ½ large onion  
\* 3 garlic cloves. thinly sliced  
\* 3 green onions, julienned  
\* 4 cups bean sprouts (heaped cups) (4 handfuls, 300g)  
\* 1 tbsp oil  

Instructions  
1. Cook 5 oz pasta according to package instructions (or until just past al dente).  
2. Rinse 4 heaped cups bean sprouts, ½ large thinly slice onion and 3 garlic cloves (thinly sliced). Lay 3 green onions onto a chopping board and cut into thirds (white, green & dark green). Julienne all three sections and set aside.   
3. Add 1 tbsp oil into a pan (a wok or cast iron pot is perfect).  Add sliced onion and the white and light green sections of green onions. Stir-fry until thinly onions have softened and add beansprouts to sauté.   
4. Once the pasta is cooked slightly past al dente, add it to the cooking beansprouts and onions. Quickly add the sliced garlic and green parts of the green onion. Pour in 1 tbsp dark soy sauce and 0.5 tbsp of light soy sauce and mix while cooking at the same time.   
5. Combine until the pasta is coated in soy sauce and evenly colored. Serve.   

RECIPE LINK: https://londonishungry.com/garlic-soy-sauce-pasta/

Here’s a method that might work well for you:

1. **Use a large pot or deep pan**: You can caramelize a big batch at once if you use a wide, heavy-bottomed pot or even a roasting pan on the stovetop. This helps the onions cook evenly without overcrowding.
2. **Low and slow**: Add a generous amount of oil or butter and cook the onions on low heat. Stir them every 10-15 minutes so they don’t stick or burn, but give them enough time to brown and release their sugars.
3. **Do it beforehand**: Caramelizing takes a while, so it’s much easier to prep them in advance. You can keep them warm in a slow cooker or even a food warmer at your stall.
4. **Storage tip**: If you’re making a lot, divide them into portions and refrigerate or freeze what you won’t need immediately. Reheat them in small batches to keep them fresh and avoid overcooking.

This way, you'll have a steady supply ready to go without having to spend hours at your stall caramelizing onions.

Lesson learned this year for me: 
1) don’t be afraid to experiment with spacing!  In a home garden it’s really not a big deal if you plant things too close, figure out what works best for your crops. 
2) don’t be afraid to pull plants to put in new ones! I just pulled a bunch of radishes and brocolli rabe to make space for tomatoes, egg plants, cucumbers, and squash. I get all sentiments and hope that I end up getting some harvest. But guess what, I have too much harvest anyways so it’s not a big deal to sacrifice those. I can always replant them in the fall! 
3) while direct seeding is recommended for a lot of spring plants, I’ve found that pests like snails and birds tend to murder my seedling and for me it’s better to transplant most things. It gives me a head start and allows the plants to get big enough to withstand pests. I am transplanting almost everything this year including cucumbers and squash! Even going to experiment with transplanting some vining beans. At worst, it’s a bit more effort on my part. But I’ve found that even though transplanting is not recommended for something, they turn out fine anyways.

Looking for research
Greetings homesteaders.

I am in the position where I will be purchasing land and a home to move into by February of 2025. I don't necessarily want to do a full-blown homestead. I work a full-time job that I actually enjoy in a field that I love. My wife is a capable gardener and would not work outside the home. What I DO want to do is produce food enough to reduce my reliance on grocery stores. I see some nasty stuff coming and I want to be prepared. Currently, here is what I am planning over the next three years:

*  Purchasing 14.5 acres in Georgia (plant hardiness zone 6-9)
* I am looking to raise some chickens. Not a ton, just five or six in order to produce enough eggs for my family of three. Hopes being that this will provide around 700 eggs a year. Additionally, they will be mostly free-range (in a large penned in yard, of course, to protect against predators), so this should allow them to help keep pests to a minimum.
* I would like a semi-self sufficient garden with the three sisters to keep soil healthy; corn, squash, and beans. This would be a moderately small garden, approximately 20x30. I would dedicate three different sections for this so that each section can fallow for two years.
* Additional garden with other basic foods; tomato, cucumber, potato, onions, peppers, lettuce, watermelon, etc. Ideally, this would be in a simplified greenhouse to protect the plants.
* Not an orchard, but a couple of fruit trees. Some apples, some peaches (it is Georgia, after all), and some lemons. I figure two apple, one peach, and one lemon (since they're both self-pollinators) should be enough to keep me having food for canning.
* Not becoming a beekeeper, but growing a bee friendly yard. I couldn't care less about having a "lawn" as I think they're horrible for the environment, but planting wildflowers and grasses that attract bees year-round, a couple bee hotels, and absolutely no pesticides/fertilizers (outside of compost).
* Composting leftovers, of course. 
* Very small vermiculture bin. Nothing crazy, probably the size of a 5-gallon bucket to get some liquid gold to add to the compost.
* I would love to get three or four goats. Again, nothing crazy because I won't be able to take care of a large herd (flock?), but I think three or four should be manageable and still provide enough milk for daily needs.

As I said, this is a longish term plan. As for the foods, I am an experienced chef, so utilizing them won't be an issue. I also hunt, which is why I am purchasing so much land, and the land has a small pond which is just large enough to stock.

So, all that being said, a couple of questions:

1. Is there a specific name for this type of homesteading?
2. Is there anything I am not thinking of that would make this lifestyle more sustainable?
3. Is three years a valid timeline to attempt to do all of this (barring finances)?
4. Any other advice?
